title: Optimize CPU request path: reduce serialization overhead, thread-pool pinning, and scheduling improvements
author: Maya Chen
description:
Context: Production serving traces and the perf bench showed a persistent CPU-side bottleneck in the request hot path for short-sequence workloads. Root causes included expensive JSON framing/serde for internal RPC, frequent allocations during batch assembly, contention in the global thread pool, and suboptimal CPU scheduling on NUMA nodes. This PR proposes a set of targeted changes to reduce per-request CPU work and stabilize tail latency.

What I changed: checklist:
- [x] Replace internal request framing from JSON to compact binary framing (small custom header + length-prefixed payload) to avoid repetitive text parsing and reduce allocations.
- [x] Introduce zero-copy buffer slices for request body handoff (single ownership transfer to worker).
- [x] Move batch-assembly off the io/accept thread into a pinned worker thread-pool that is NUMA-aware.
- [x] Add CPU affinity pinning configuration for the serving worker pool; default pins on socket boundaries for multi-socket hosts.
- [x] Convert the global thread-pool to a hierarchical pool: accept/io threads -> batch-assembly workers (pinned) -> kernel execution workers.
- [x] Replace a contended std::mutex in KV cache access path with an optimistic read-side fast path + slow-path locked upgrade for writes.
- [x] Small scheduling changes: use SCHED_BATCH where appropriate for long-running GPU-to-CPU copy workers, keep latency-sensitive workers in default policy.
- [x] Add benchmarks and microbench tests under perf/ to track latency and CPU usage.

Description: The changes aim to cut repeated syscall/parse overhead and reduce cross-socket cache-coherence churn by keeping hot CPU work on a pinned set of cores. The binary framing eliminates repetitive JSON tokenization for the most common internal RPC messages between the front-end HTTP layer and the serving runtime; a short compatibility shim is provided for older agents. Batch assembly was a source of allocations and lock contention when assembling incoming requests into continuous batches; moving this to pinned workers reduces scheduling jitter on the accept threads and allows tighter control of batching latency vs throughput. The KV cache fast-path reduces spin and waiter counts under read-heavy workloads common in production.

Risk and rollout plan: changes are behind feature flags (runtime.cpu_path_opt_v1). Default is off for Dedicated until we validate on several instance types. Rollout plan: canary in staging -> opt-in on limited Dedicated pools -> gradual ramp across regions with metrics monitoring in Console.

Related: ENG-1420 (cpu-request-path bottleneck), ENG-1435 (batching regressions), SUP-912 (customer incident #2026-02-08).

release_notes: Performance: Optimized CPU request path to reduce serialization overhead and scheduling contention. Binary framing, zero-copy handoff, NUMA-aware pinned worker pool, and optimistic KV-cache reads reduce p50/p95 latency for short-sequence workloads. Rollout behind runtime.cpu_path_opt_v1 feature flag.
perf_summary: p50 latency reduced from 28ms -> 16ms (approx 43% lower) on c6-standard-equivalent test agents for short sequences (<=64 tokens)
CPU user/sys time for request path reduced ~30% in microbench (less context switching and fewer allocations)
Tail jitter (99th) saw improvements but varies by instance topology; NUMA pinning eliminated cross-socket slow tails in multi-socket tests
motivation: Reduce per-request CPU overhead and variance for short-sequence inference workloads by addressing serialization, allocation churn, and thread scheduling/affinity. This increases throughput and lowers unit cost for common production workloads.
